title: Binary Trees, Part 1
note: No visual for this lecture; straight transcript teaching, six chunks. No source defects found on a close read — the mixed-metaphor humor about leaves having no children and the poor root having no parent is Demaine's own delivery, not a transcription slip, and is worth keeping in the emphasis rather than smoothed away, since it is how the terminology actually sticks. One inaudible audience turn (a bare 'AUDIENCE:' at the transcript's line 299) falls inside chunk 3; it is a request to recap runtimes, and Demaine's reply carries the content the way the other empty turns did in l05. This lecture builds toward the sequence/set implementations promised for the next lecture (l07) but does not reach them — today's payoff is bounding everything by tree height h, with the promise that h becomes O(log n) next time; the emphasis says so rather than implying today's operations are already fast in the worst case. Chunk indexes come from scripts/lesson.mjs and must stay in sync with the bundle.

sections.topic: ERIK DEMAINE: All right, let's get started. Welcome back to 006. Today w
sections.emphasis: Open with the motivation, since it sets up why binary trees are worth building at all. Recap the two interfaces from earlier in the course and name exactly what was missing: for sequences, nothing supported insert-in-the-middle or delete-in-the-middle efficiently — linked lists can't even reach the middle without linear time, and arrays reach it fine but shifting on a change is expensive. For sets, hash tables are great at exact find/insert/delete but useless at find-previous and find-next, and the one structure that answers those, a sorted array, can't be kept sorted efficiently under insertions and deletions. Binary trees are the fix for both, and the promise is logarithmic time — but say honestly that today does not reach log n; today gets every operation down to O(h), the height of the tree, and next lecture is what guarantees h itself is O(log n). Then define the structure precisely: a node has a parent pointer, a left-child pointer, a right-child pointer, and an item; the root is the unique node with no parent, and Demaine's own line about it — 'it's sad to have no parents, but here you go' — is worth keeping, since the running joke about leaves having no children is exactly how the vocabulary sticks. State the key invariant plainly: parent is always the inverse of left or right, so walking node.left then .parent returns to node. Close with the definitions the rest of the lecture builds on: the subtree of a node is that node plus all its descendants; ancestors are parent, grandparent, and so on up to the root; depth of a node counts the edges on the unique upward path to the root (so the root has depth 0); height of a node is the number of edges on the longest downward path in its subtree (so every leaf has height 0), and the height of the whole tree, called h, is the height of the root — the quantity today's entire lecture is measured against.

quiz.question: Demaine says today's lecture gets every operation to run in O(h) time, the height of the tree — not yet O(log n). Why is that distinction important?
options: O(h) is only as good as O(log n) if the tree is kept shallow; a badly shaped tree — like one built entirely from right pointers, which is really a linked list — can have height close to n, and guaranteeing shallowness is exactly what next lecture adds
It is not an important distinction — h and log n are just two names for the same quantity in every binary tree
O(h) is always worse than O(log n), so today's operations are strictly slower than what hash tables already provide
quiz.explain: Demaine says it directly: a tree built like a linked list, using only right pointers, has height close to n, so O(h) there is really O(n) — no better than the structures binary trees are supposed to replace. h only becomes O(log n) once the tree is kept balanced, which is the job of the next lecture, not this one. Today's operations are correct and bounded by height, but 'fast' is a promise this lecture sets up rather than delivers.

sections.topic: AUDIENCE: A couple of questions. Is the height of C-- of node C is 0 or-
sections.emphasis: Close the height/depth definitions with the audience's clarifying question, and keep the answer crisp: height counts edges, not vertices or nodes, so a leaf like node C has height 0 — there are zero edges on any downward path from a leaf, since there is nowhere to go. Note the terminology precisely: 'height of the tree' means the height of the root, but 'depth of the tree' is not a defined phrase — only individual nodes have a depth; the two numbers happen to coincide only in the sense that the tree's height equals its maximum node depth. Then introduce the tool the rest of the lecture is built on: traversal order, also called in-order traversal, a single total order over every node in the tree. Define it recursively and make the recursive structure land, not just the example: for every node X, everything in X.left comes before X in the order, and everything in X.right comes after X — apply that at every node, all the way down, and it uniquely defines an order. Walk Demaine's worked example (F, D, B, E, A, C) enough to make the recursion concrete: C comes after A because it's in A's right subtree, while everything else is in A's left subtree and so comes before A, and the same rule recurses at B, D and every other node. State the simple recursive algorithm for computing it — to iterate a subtree rooted at X, iterate the left subtree, output X, then iterate the right subtree — and note it is exactly the in-order traversal many learners have already seen, just re-derived from the ordering rule rather than handed down as a recipe. Close on why this order matters: it is never stored explicitly (that comes next), but a sequence is represented by making the traversal order the sequence order, and a set is represented by making it the sorted order of keys.

quiz.question: In-order traversal is defined by one recursive rule: for every node X, everything in X.left comes before X, and everything in X.right comes after X. Why does applying that same rule at every node produce a single, unambiguous order over the whole tree?
options: Because the rule is applied recursively at every node, it recursively orders every subtree the same way, so nesting the left-subtree order, then X, then the right-subtree order at each level composes into one consistent total order with no ties or contradictions
It does not always produce one order — ties are broken arbitrarily whenever two nodes have the same depth
The order only works for trees where every node has exactly two children; a node missing a child breaks the recursion
quiz.explain: The recursion bottoms out cleanly: a leaf's subtree order is just itself, and at every node above it, the rule places the whole left-subtree order before the node and the whole right-subtree order after it, with no ambiguity about where any node lands relative to any other. A missing child is simply an empty subtree that contributes nothing to the order — the recursive algorithm (iterate left, output X, iterate right) works whether X has zero, one, or two children, which is exactly why it is the same algorithm learners may already know as in-order traversal.

sections.topic: AUDIENCE: A node can be only part of one subtree, right?
sections.emphasis: Handle the audience's misconception directly, because it is a natural one: a node belongs to many subtrees at once — the subtree rooted at itself, and the subtree rooted at each of its ancestors — but the operation about to be defined, subtree-first, only cares about the one subtree that a given node roots. Define subtree-first precisely: among all nodes in the subtree rooted at a given node, which comes first in traversal order? Walk the answer the way Demaine draws it out of the class rather than just stating it: go left as far as possible — node = node.left, repeatedly, until node becomes none — then undo the last step and return that last non-none node, the leftmost node in the subtree. Say why that is correct, not just how to compute it: by the traversal-order rule, everything in a node's left subtree comes before it, so as long as a left child exists, the true first element must be somewhere in there; the moment there is no left child left to follow, that node has nothing before it in its own subtree, so it must be first. Then move to the more interesting operation, successor: given a node, which node comes next in the overall traversal order? Establish the two cases cleanly, since the rest of insert and delete are built on this split. Case one: if the node has a right child, the successor is the leftmost node of that right subtree — exactly subtree-first applied to node.right — because everything in the right subtree comes after the node, and the first of those is nearest. Case two, when there is no right child, is the harder one and is worth setting up here even if the full argument lands next: walk upward via node.parent until the step taken is 'up a left branch' — that is, until node is the left child of its parent — and that parent is the successor.

quiz.question: Subtree-first is computed by following node = node.left repeatedly until node is none, then returning the last node before that happened. Why does that procedure return the correct node — the first in the subtree's traversal order?
options: By the traversal-order rule, everything in a node's left subtree comes before it; so as long as a left child exists there is always something earlier, and the walk only stops at a node with no left child left to follow — which by the same rule has nothing earlier in its own subtree, making it first
It works because binary trees are always height-balanced, so the leftmost path is guaranteed to be the shortest one
It is really an approximation — it finds A node with no left child, but there could be several equally valid 'first' nodes in a subtree
quiz.explain: The traversal-order rule is what makes the walk correct, not any balance assumption — a badly shaped tree still has this property. Any node with a left child has something ordered before it, by definition, so the search must continue leftward. The walk terminates exactly at the one node in the subtree that has no left child, and that same rule says such a node has nothing before it within its own subtree, so it is uniquely first — traversal order is a strict total order, so there cannot be more than one 'first' node.

sections.emphasis: Answer the audience's question about the successor's upward walk by restating the invariant plainly: 'placed into the traversal order' means implicitly, in the structure of the tree itself — the traversal order is never materialized as an explicit array; it lives only in the shape of the pointers, which is exactly what makes it affordable to maintain. Say why that matters before moving on, since it is the whole reason binary trees exist: an explicit array of the order would cost linear time to update on every insertion, but the tree structure lets these operations cost only the height of the tree, h — except full iteration through the whole order, which is unavoidably O(n) since it has to touch every node. Note in passing that a full recap of these bounds is what the next, inaudible audience turn is asking for, and Demaine's answer is exactly this summary — subtree-first costs O(h), successor costs O(h) since it either does one subtree-first call or walks up at most the height of the tree. Then move to the first structural change of the lecture: insertion. To insert a new node right after an existing node in traversal order, there are two cases, and both cost only constant work beyond a successor-style call. Case one: if the existing node has no right child, attach the new node as its right child directly — nothing else needs to move. Case two: if the node does have a right child, attach the new node as the left child of the node's successor — and the key fact that makes this always legal is that the successor, having been found by going right once and then left as far as possible, is guaranteed to have no left child of its own, so there is always room. Walk Demaine's two examples — inserting G before E, and inserting H after A — enough to make both cases concrete, and land the runtime: insertion costs O(h), the same bound as successor, because it is successor plus one constant-time pointer attachment.

quiz.question: When inserting a new node after an existing node that already has a right child, the new node is attached as the left child of the node's successor. Why is that attachment always legal — why is there always room?
options: The successor was found by going right once, then left as far as possible, which by definition means it has no left child of its own — so attaching the new node there never overwrites an existing pointer
It is not always legal; occasionally the successor already has a left child, and that case has to be handled separately
Because the tree is kept balanced, every node always has room for one more child somewhere nearby
quiz.explain: Subtree-first — the walk used to compute the successor's identity — stops exactly at the node with no left child, since that is the definition of being leftmost in a subtree. So whenever case two applies, the successor node is guaranteed empty on its left side, and attaching the new node there is always safe; there is no third case to handle. This is exactly why insertion only costs one successor-style walk (O(h)) plus one constant-time pointer set, with no searching for a free slot.

sections.emphasis: The audience turn here is a one-word transcription check ('new' not 'node'); move past it quickly and start deletion. Give the base case first, since it is genuinely simple: deleting a leaf just detaches it from its parent — Demaine's example is erasing F, which has no children, so there is nothing else to fix up. The harder case is deleting a node that is not a leaf, and the running example is deleting the root, A, which has both children. State the trick precisely, since it is the heart of the operation: you cannot just erase a node with children without disconnecting the tree, so instead you swap the deleted node's item with its predecessor's (or successor's) item, then recursively delete from the predecessor's old position — which is strictly lower in the tree, since a predecessor reached by going left-then-rightmost is always further down. Walk Demaine's example precisely, since the mechanics matter: delete A by finding its predecessor E (leftmost subtree, then rightmost as far as possible), swapping A and E's items, and now the 'problem' has moved to where E's item used to be; since that spot is not yet a leaf either, repeat — find its predecessor G, swap again — until the item being deleted has moved all the way down to an actual leaf, which is then simply detached as in the base case. State the general case split precisely: if the node being deleted has a left child, its predecessor is guaranteed to be inside that left subtree (so strictly lower), so swap with the predecessor and recurse there; if it has a right child but no left child, use the successor instead, by the same logic. Land the runtime: because every step of this process moves strictly downward in the tree, and each step does only constant work besides finding the predecessor or successor, the total cost of a deletion is O(h), the height of the tree.

quiz.question: Deleting a non-leaf node swaps its item with its predecessor's item, then recursively deletes from the predecessor's old position. Why is the predecessor guaranteed to be lower in the tree than the node being deleted, when that node has a left child?
options: The predecessor of a node with a left child is found by going left once and then right as far as possible, which lands strictly inside that left subtree — necessarily deeper than the node itself
It is not guaranteed — sometimes the predecessor is an ancestor, and the recursion has to walk upward instead
The predecessor is always the node's direct left child, one level down, regardless of that child's own subtree
quiz.explain: The predecessor-finding walk (the mirror of subtree-first) goes left once into the left subtree and then as far right as possible inside it — every step of that walk goes deeper, so the predecessor always lands strictly below the original node whenever a left child exists. That guarantee is exactly why repeatedly swapping-and-recursing is guaranteed to terminate: the 'hole' being deleted moves strictly downward every time, until it reaches an actual leaf and the base case applies, bounding the whole process by the tree's height.

sections.topic: AUDIENCE: Why do you do a right child to C, but it's like you never had
sections.emphasis: Answer the audience's confusion about the deletion example precisely, because it names something easy to miss: the circles — the physical nodes — never move during a delete; only the items stored inside them change places. So calling a node 'E' or 'A' after a swap is just naming it by whatever item currently lives there, not tracking which physical node it originally was. State the blunt principle behind this, in Demaine's own words: trees will not preserve identity or connections across a delete — the operation is allowed to relabel what a node 'is,' and that's a deliberate design choice, not a bug, since without it deletion could not be done in O(h) time at all. Then close the lecture by connecting today's tool back to the two interfaces from the opening: to represent a sequence, make the traversal order equal to the sequence order directly; to represent a set, make the traversal order equal to the sorted order of keys — and name this special case precisely, since the term recurs constantly afterward: a binary tree whose traversal order is sorted by key is a binary search tree, with the BST property that every key in a node's left subtree is less than the node's key, and every key in its right subtree is greater, recursively at every node. Walk the search example the way Demaine does it — searching for key 13 by comparing at each node and going left or right — and land the two related, more subtle queries: if the search falls off the tree, the last node visited while heading right is the answer to find-previous, and the last node visited while heading left is one step from find-next — apply successor from that last-visited-while-left node, or predecessor from the last-visited-while-right node, to get the other. Close honestly on what is still missing: today only covers the set-shaped operations; turning this into a full sequence structure with fast get_at is next lecture's work.

quiz.question: In a binary search tree, searching for a key that is not present 'falls off' the tree at some point. How do you recover find-previous or find-next from where the search fell off?
options: The last node visited while the search was heading right (comparing the missing key as larger) is the answer to find-previous; the last node visited while heading left is one step from find-next by applying successor to it
You have to restart the search from the root and run a full traversal to find the neighboring keys
Find-previous and find-next are undefined once a search misses — the BST property only supports exact-match search
quiz.explain: The BST property means every comparison during the search correctly separates smaller keys (left) from larger keys (right); the point where the search falls off the tree is exactly the boundary between the previous and next keys in sorted order. The last node the search moved right past is smaller than the target and nothing closer exists, so it is the previous item directly; symmetrically, applying successor (or predecessor, depending on direction) to the appropriate last-visited node recovers the other neighbor — all without restarting the search or touching nodes outside the search path.
